prompt: Which of these literals holds a real tab character between `a` and `b`?
hint: Where does a backslash start an escape?

choices.why: Between backquotes nothing is an escape, so this is four characters: `a`, a backslash, `t`, `b`.
Right. In double quotes `\t` is one character, the tab.

choices.text: `"a\\tb"`, since the doubled backslash makes the escape stronger
choices.why: `\\` is an escaped backslash, so the string holds a backslash followed by `t`.

choices.text: `'a\tb'`, because single quotes keep escapes too
choices.why: Single quotes make a rune literal, and three characters in one is refused, as lesson 8 showed.

prompt: What happens with `path := "C:\new\table"`?
hint: Are `\n` and `\t` escapes Go knows?

choices.text: The compiler refuses it with unknown escape
choices.why: That was `\d`, which is not an escape. `\n` and `\t` are, so this compiles.

choices.text: It compiles, and the string holds a newline and a tab
choices.why: Right. Nothing complains, `go vet` exited 0, and `fmt.Println` printed `C:` on a line of its own.

choices.text: It compiles, but `go vet` reports the suspicious escapes
choices.why: `go vet` printed nothing and exited 0; the escapes are valid, so there is nothing for it to see.

choices.text: It compiles, and the path is stored exactly as typed
choices.why: That is what the raw literal `` `C:\new\table` `` does. Double quotes turned two of the backslashes into escapes.

hint: In a raw literal each backslash is one byte.

prompt: Which of these lines does the compiler refuse?
hint: One backslash is followed by a letter that is not an escape.

`\\` is a valid escape for one backslash, so the string is `\d+` and it compiles.
Right: unknown escape. `\d` means something to a regular expression and nothing to Go.

choices.text: `p := "\x41"`, since a hexadecimal escape has to name a whole code point
choices.why: `\x41` is one byte, 65, and printed `A` in `~/strings-lit`.

prompt: `s := "hello"`. What does Go do with `s[0] = 'H'`?
hint: Can a string's bytes change?

choices.text: Changes the first byte of `s` in place
choices.why: That is a C array. A Go string's bytes are fixed when it is made.

choices.text: Compiles, then panics when the line runs
choices.why: The refusal comes earlier: it is a compile error, and nothing runs.

choices.text: Refuses to compile it: cannot assign to `s[0]`
choices.why: Right. `s[0]` can be read and never assigned.

choices.text: Changes a copy of the string, and `s` keeps saying hello
choices.why: No copy is made either: the assignment is refused before the program exists.

prompt: `t := s`, then `s = "H" + s[1:]`, with `s` starting as `"hello, world"`. What does `fmt.Println(t)` print?
hint: Did anything write into the bytes `t` refers to?

choices.text: `Hello, world`, because `t` and `s` share their bytes
choices.why: They did share bytes, but `s` was given new bytes by `+`; the old ones never changed.

choices.text: `hello, world`
choices.why: Right. `s` now holds a new string, and `t` still holds the old one.

choices.text: Nothing: the assignment to `s` is a compile error
choices.why: Assigning a new string to a variable is allowed; only writing into a string's bytes is refused.

choices.text: An empty line, since the old string was freed when `s` moved on
choices.why: Memory that something still points to is never freed; `t` keeps the old bytes alive.

prompt: On the lab's amd64 machine, what does `unsafe.Sizeof(book)` give for a string holding a whole book?
hint: What did it give for `"a"`?

choices.text: The number of bytes in the book
choices.why: That is `len(book)`. The string value only points at those bytes.

choices.text: 24, a pointer, a length and a capacity
choices.why: A string has no capacity, since nothing can be appended to it in place; it is two words, not three.

choices.text: 16: a pointer and a length, 8 bytes each
choices.why: Right, whatever the text; it gave 16 for `"a"` as well.

choices.text: 8, the size of the pointer to the text alone
choices.why: The length travels with the pointer, which is why `len` costs nothing; together they are 16.

prompt: A program reads a 1 GB log into a string `log` and keeps only `first := log[:80]` in a map that lives as long as the program. How much of the log stays in memory?
hint: What does a substring point into?

choices.text: 80 bytes, because slicing copies the part it takes
choices.why: Slicing copies nothing: `w` started seven bytes after `t`, inside the same bytes.

choices.text: The whole gigabyte, since `first` points into it; `strings.Clone(first)` would keep 80 bytes
choices.why: Right. That is the case `go doc strings.Clone` names: retaining a small substring of a much larger string.

choices.text: None of it: `first` stops being valid once `log` is no longer used
choices.why: That is a dangling pointer in C. Go keeps the bytes alive for as long as anything points into them.

choices.text: 80 bytes, because the garbage collector trims what no substring covers
choices.why: The collector frees whole allocations, never part of one; the gigabyte is one allocation.

prompt: Why did 100,000 rounds of `s += "ab"` take seconds when a `strings.Builder` took milliseconds?
hint: What does `+` do with the string built so far?

choices.text: Each `+=` copied the whole string built so far into new memory
choices.why: Right: 2 bytes, then 4, up to 200,000, about 10 billion bytes moved in all.

choices.text: Each `+=` checked that the result was valid UTF-8
choices.why: `+` checks nothing; a string can hold any bytes. The cost is the copying.

choices.text: The `for range` loop is slow, and the Builder version avoided it
choices.why: Both programs ran the same loop 100,000 times; only what happened inside differed.

choices.text: Strings are compared on every `+=`, and comparing grows with length
choices.why: Nothing is compared. `+=` builds a new string and copies both sides into it.

prompt: `s := "café"`. What is `s[3]`?
hint: Indexing a string counts in bytes.

choices.text: The rune `'é'`
choices.why: `é` starts at byte 3 but takes two bytes; indexing gives only the first of them.

choices.text: The byte 195, the first half of `é`
choices.why: Right: a `uint8`, which `%c` drew as the wrong character, `Ã`.

choices.text: The string `"é"`
choices.why: An index gives one byte, never a string; a string would come from slicing, `s[3:5]`.

choices.text: The byte 102, the `f`
choices.why: That is `s[2]`. Indexes start at 0, so `s[3]` is the fourth byte.

prompt: `s := "café"`. Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: `é` is two bytes.

choices.text: `len(s)` is 5
choices.why: Yes: three ASCII bytes and two for `é`.

choices.text: `utf8.RuneCountInString(s)` is 4
choices.why: Yes: four runes, the precomposed `é` being one.

choices.text: `s[:4]` is valid UTF-8
choices.why: It ends in the lone byte `\xc3`, and `utf8.ValidString` said `false`.

choices.text: `s[4]` is the letter `é`
choices.why: `s[4]` is 169, the second half of `é`, and a byte at that.

prompt: What does `strings.Index("café au lait", "au")` return?
hint: Count bytes, not characters.

choices.text: 5, the number of characters before `au`
choices.why: Five characters, but `é` is two bytes, and `strings` answers in bytes.

choices.text: 6, the offset in bytes
choices.why: Right: c, a, f, two bytes of `é` and a space come first.

choices.text: 7, counting from 1
choices.why: Offsets start at 0, as indexes do.

choices.text: 4, the number of runes in `café`
choices.why: That counts `café` only and in runes; the answer is a byte offset into the whole string.

prompt: A server receives a name over the network and `utf8.RuneCountInString(name)` returns 10. What does that tell you?
hint: What did it answer for `"\xff\xfe"`?

choices.text: The name is valid UTF-8 with 10 characters
choices.why: Neither follows: invalid bytes count as one rune each, and runes are not characters.

choices.text: The name is 10 bytes long
choices.why: `len` would tell you that; runes and bytes match only for ASCII.

choices.text: The name holds no invalid bytes, or the count would be an error
choices.why: It returns one number and no error; `"\xff\xfe"` gave 2.

choices.text: Little until `utf8.ValidString(name)` is true; then it has 10 runes
choices.why: Right. Check validity first, and remember that runes are still not characters as a reader sees them.

prompt: A screen shows the first 9 bytes of a name with `name[:9]`. What goes wrong for `"Conceição Silva"`?
hint: Count the bytes of `ç` and `ã`.

choices.text: It panics, because `name` contains letters outside ASCII
choices.why: Slicing within the length never panics, whatever the bytes are; the result is just wrong.

choices.text: It returns the first 9 characters, `Conceição`
choices.why: That would need 11 bytes, since `ç` and `ã` take two each.

choices.text: It cuts `ã` in half and the result is not valid UTF-8
choices.why: Right: `Conceiç` and the lone first byte of `ã`, the same cut as `s[:4]` on `café`.

choices.text: It does not compile, since slicing a string needs the `utf8` package
choices.why: Slicing is part of the language; `s[:3]` and `s[:4]` compiled with no import.
